title: Indians Form Britain's Largest Foreign Workforce as Migrants Take Most New Jobs
excerpt: A Centre for Social Justice report found only 734,000 of 3.7 million additional UK payroll jobs since 2014 went to British nationals, while HMRC data shows Indian nationals held 1,029,300 jobs in December 2025 — more than any other foreign nationality.
body:
• Of 3.7 million additional payroll jobs in Britain between 2014 and 2025, only 734,000 went to British nationals, the Centre for Social Justice found — four in five went to foreign nationals.
  • Indian nationals held 1,029,300 payroll jobs in December 2025, the largest number of any foreign nationality and 16% of all payroll jobs held by non-UK nationals, according to HMRC data cited by the report.
  • Most growth came after 2020: non-EU payroll jobs rose 2.1 million while the out-of-work benefit caseload rose 2.3 million.
  • For Indians in Britain: the figures put the community at the center of a live policy fight over settlement and welfare, including a government plan to lengthen the route to indefinite leave to remain — check your status timeline before assuming the old five-year path applies.

Foreign nationals took four in five of the additional payroll jobs created in Britain between 2014 and the end of 2025, and Indian nationals now hold more of those jobs than any other foreign nationality, according to a Centre for Social Justice (CSJ) report covered by The Times of India. The report, State of Dependency, is the first output of the think tank's Welfare 2030 inquiry, chaired by former work and pensions secretary Sir Iain Duncan Smith.

The numbers behind the headline

The CSJ analyzed HM Revenue and Customs PAYE data and found payrolled employments rose by about 3.7 million over the period, from 28.3 million in July 2014 to 32 million by December 2025. British nationals accounted for 734,000 of the increase. EU nationals accounted for 408,000, and jobs held by non-EU nationals rose by about 2.5 million. Within that total, HMRC data cited in the reporting shows Indian nationals held 1,029,300 jobs in December 2025 — 16% of all payroll jobs held by non-UK nationals — an increase of 728,200 since 2014. The full findings are on the Centre for Social Justice report page.

Growth concentrated after the pandemic

Most of the shift happened after January 2020. Non-EU payroll positions rose 2.1 million in that period, while payroll jobs held by British nationals fell in nine of the UK's 12 nations and regions, including a drop of 53,000 in Scotland and 26,500 in London. London added 465,200 non-EU payroll jobs and the South East 284,500. By sector, health and social work accounted for 29% of the increase in non-EU payroll employment, followed by administrative services at 16%, hospitality at 12%, and retail at 10%. Over the same years, the number of people receiving out-of-work benefits rose by 2.3 million, and about 6.7 million people now receive at least one out-of-work benefit. The working-age benefit bill is set to reach £136.1 billion in 2026/27.

"Ministers have repeatedly pulled the easy lever of immigration rather than providing a better deal for left behind communities."

— Sir Iain Duncan Smith, chair of the Welfare 2030 inquiry

What the report argues — and what it does not show

The CSJ argues that successive governments used migration to expand headline GDP — a practice it calls "human quantitative easing" — while domestic worklessness grew, and it wants welfare, immigration and regional policy reformed together. Opposition politicians echoed that framing, while a government spokesperson responded that most of the workforce is made up of UK nationals, pointed to a new skills-based migration system, and cited £3.5 billion to help disabled people move toward work, The Sun reported. The CSJ figures describe who held the additional jobs by nationality; on their own they do not prove that a migrant worker took a specific job from a specific British applicant.

Why it matters for the Indian community in Britain

Indians are not a footnote in this data — at just over one million payroll jobs, they are the single largest foreign workforce in the country, concentrated in the health service, technology and professional sectors as well as the lower-paid care, hospitality and retail roles where much of the post-2020 growth occurred. That scale cuts both ways: it shows deep economic integration, and it makes Indian workers the most exposed if the debate produces tighter rules. The Home Secretary has already announced plans to double the standard qualifying period for indefinite leave to remain. Anyone in Britain on a work route should verify their settlement timeline against current Home Office guidance rather than rely on the timetable in place when they arrived.

What happens next

State of Dependency is a think-tank report, not government policy, but its chair is a former cabinet minister and its framing is already shaping opposition attacks and government defenses. Watch for whether its recommendations — linking welfare reform, skills investment and migration settings — are picked up in the next budget and in the government's response to the Welfare 2030 inquiry's later reports.
